chapters.title: Errors
chapters.hook: Why did the scolded flight cadet seem cured while the praised one slipped?
chapters.counterintuition: Why does experience sometimes teach the wrong lesson? A swing back toward average can look like proof that praise failed or punishment worked.
chapters.tryThisNow: Within the next 24 hours, the first time a result feels obvious, pre-write two replies: "This may be skill" and "This may be noise." Name the difference.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When results swing sharply, name the pattern before you praise or blame: regression and sampling noise can make a vivid story feel like proof too soon.

breakdown.fastRead:
Miles watches a flight instructor point at two cadets and draw the wrong moral. The praised cadet flies worse next time. The scolded cadet flies better. It feels as if praise softened one pilot and anger fixed the other. The missing fact is regression to the mean: a very high or low result often moves closer to average on the next try. Variation can wear the mask of a lesson.

Kahneman's early work made errors useful by giving them shape. The issue was not that people were foolish. It was that experience can hand them a neat story when chance is doing part of the work. Once you name the pattern, you can stop turning every swing into praise, blame, or character.
breakdown.deepRead:
Regression starts with a simple picture: one extreme result sits far from a person's usual level. The next result has many ways to land closer to normal. If Leon sees only the two runs, he may give credit to the speech between them. If he sees the whole spread of runs, the story changes.

The Israeli Air Force instructors had a strong reason to trust their own eyes. They had watched flight cadets improve after harsh words and slip after praise. In a teaching room, that felt like hard-earned wisdom. Kahneman's move was not to call the instructors cruel. He separated the feedback from the swing in performance. A cadet who just flew unusually badly had room to look better next time. A cadet who just flew unusually well had room to fall back. The lesson was not moral. It was statistical.

Paul Meehl pressed the same nerve from another side. In Clinical versus Statistical Prediction, published in 1954, he showed that simple actuarial methods often beat rich clinical impressions. A score humbles a story. The clinician's picture may be vivid and humane, but a scored rule can still predict better.

Small samples add a third trap. A few cases can look steady, then fail when a replication asks for the same result again. At Hebrew University, sampling variability was not a dry term. It was the reason a careful plan could feel strong while resting on too little data. The move is to ask what pattern could make the answer feel obvious.
breakdown.fullRead:
Iris can see why the instructors resisted. They were not inventing a superstition from thin air. They were watching aircraft, cadets, praise, and bad landings in real time. Their mistake came from a close view, not from a lazy mind. A vivid sequence can feel like a cause because the human eye likes a before and an after.

Kahneman's useful turn was to treat the error as a thing with parts. First comes an extreme result. Then comes a second result that lands nearer the usual level. Then the mind assigns credit to whatever happened between the two. In the flight case, that thing was praise or criticism. In another setting, it might be a new checklist, a coach's speech, or a stern email. The shape is the same. The story arrives before the math is invited.

The same shape helps explain why Meehl mattered. Paul Meehl did not say trained judgment was worthless. His clinical-versus-statistical work asked for a score against another way to predict. A clinician could hold a rich picture of a person and still lose to an actuarial method. That is a painful finding because the expert's story may contain true details. The question is whether those details improve the forecast.

Small samples make the pain worse because they can look clean. Lucas can run a small Hebrew University study, see a pattern, and feel the work is ready. Statistical power asks a plainer question: is there enough data for the result to survive a second try? Small samples can fake a loud signal. A failed replication may be the first honest sign that the first result was too thin.

A reader can use the same check in ordinary life. A sales call goes badly, then the next one goes well after a new script. A clinic tries a new intake question with six patients and likes the first pattern. A supervisor trusts a rich interview more than a scored form. None of these stories is worthless. Each one needs a rival explanation before it becomes a rule.

This is why the weak takeaway misses the best part. Calling people irrational turns a pattern into an insult. A better question asks which fact the mind is missing. Is the result extreme? Is the sample small? Is the expert impression being scored against a rule? These questions slow the story before it hardens.

This move breaks in a true one-case emergency. If a nurse sees a patient stop breathing, she should not pause to wonder whether the sample is too small. She acts. Structured error helps when you have a pattern to check, a forecast to score, or a later result to compare. It cannot replace direct action when the next minute is the whole case.

examples.title: Cadet Chalk Lesson
examples.scenario: Instructor Miles erases the praise column in an Israeli Air Force classroom while the class still argues over flight cadets. A clipboard lists praise after one run and criticism after another. Miles has chalk dust on his sleeve and one live choice: teach reinforcement as a moral rule, or mark regression to the mean beside the two cadet runs.
examples.whatToDo: Miles redraws the two cadet runs as part of a wider spread. He names regression to the mean before anyone treats praise or scolding as the cause.
examples.whyItMatters: The class can still discuss feedback, but the first lesson is cleaner: a swing toward average is not proof that harsh words taught better than praise.

examples.title: Two Flights Apart
examples.scenario: Leon is staring at the worse second run before anyone mentions the first one. Earlier, the Israeli Air Force cadet had flown far above his usual line and earned praise on the tarmac. Now the instructor wants to drop praise from training. Leon keeps both runs on the board and asks whether regression to the mean fits better than a lesson about softness.
examples.whatToDo: Leon compares the cadet with his own usual level before judging the praise. He treats the later dip as evidence to check, not a verdict.
examples.whyItMatters: The before-and-later view protects the instructor from learning the wrong rule from two vivid flights that sit far from the cadet's norm.

examples.title: Meehl Score Exchange
examples.scenario: The pencil's scratch sounds too loud in the Hebrew University seminar room as student Marguerite copies Clinical versus Statistical Prediction. Iris taps 1954 beside Paul Meehl's name on the handout. "The clinician saw more," Marguerite says. "The actuarial method scored more," Iris answers. Marguerite leaves the next line blank.
examples.whatToDo: Marguerite writes the two forecasts side by side, then asks Iris to score them against the outcome instead of voting for the fuller story.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange keeps expertise in the room while forcing it to meet a count. Prediction gets better when feeling is compared with a rule.

examples.title: Power Before Pride
examples.scenario: "Use the first clean result," Iris reads at the top of her Hebrew University notes, then stops speaking. The sample is small. The pattern looks bright. Maybe replication will be fine. Maybe sampling variability is posing as a discovery. She writes statistical power in the margin and feels the pull to call the result real before the numbers deserve it.
examples.whatToDo: Iris keeps the finding provisional and checks the study size before treating the clean pattern as a stable result.
examples.whyItMatters: Her private pause turns excitement into a testable plan. A small sample can tempt careful people, not just careless ones.

examples.title: Replication Budget
examples.scenario: The shared calendar invite slides across Lucas's screen with three empty blocks for the Hebrew University project. One block could polish the small-sample result; one could recruit more cases; one could plan replication. Sampling variability is the quiet cost in each box. Before any study runs, Lucas has to decide which hour gets protected.
examples.whatToDo: Lucas protects the replication block first, then assigns time to sample size and only later to polish. He plans around statistical power, not excitement.
examples.whyItMatters: The calendar choice makes the abstract risk visible. If time goes only to the striking result, the team may dress up noise as signal.

examples.title: Two Bad Forecasts
examples.scenario: Every forecast on Levi's sheet leaves someone uneasy at the hospital nurses' station. Frances trusts the clinician's full interview, but Paul Meehl's 1954 work says the actuarial method may predict better. Levi is torn between two bad risks: follow the story and ignore the score, or follow the score and flatten detail that feels human.
examples.whatToDo: Levi asks Frances to score both forecasts against the same outcome. He refuses to crown either the story or the actuarial method without a check.
examples.whyItMatters: The hard choice is not expert versus humane. It is whether a prediction has earned trust by beating a rival method on the same case.

questions.prompt: "The cadet improved because I yelled after the bad run," Leon says after a training flight. Which reply best catches the error?
choices: The bad run is memorable, so Leon should treat the next flight as the instructor's best evidence.
The criticism might matter, so Leon should compare only cadets who heard the same words.
The bad run may have been extreme, so Leon should check regression before crediting the yelling.
questions.explanation: The flight case warns that punishment can look effective when an extreme bad run moves closer to average. The memorable story is not enough without the mechanism.

questions.prompt: A coach praises a player after an unusually strong drill, then sees an ordinary drill next. What should the coach infer first?
choices: The first drill may have been unusually high, so a move toward average needs no teaching effect.
The praise likely weakened effort, so the coach should use sharper words after strong drills.
The player's name makes the case concrete, so the coach can trust the two-drill pattern.
questions.explanation: Regression says an extreme result often drifts toward average on a later try. Names and vivid order help memory, but they do not prove praise caused the dip.

questions.prompt: "Our senior clinician saw subtle clues the score missed," Marguerite says during a forecast review. What does Meehl's work press her to ask?
choices: Whether the biography of the clinician explains why the forecast felt so convincing.
Whether the subtle clues make the clinical story richer than any simple rule.
Whether the clinical forecast beats a statistical rule when both are scored.
questions.explanation: Meehl's pressure point is comparison. Rich judgment may contain true detail, but the forecast still needs to be tested against a scored statistical method.

questions.prompt: Iris sees a striking result from eight cases and wants to present it as stable. Which next step best fits the sampling warning?
choices: She should treat the profession as special and leave the sample question inside the original setting.
She should trust the clean pattern because a careful researcher would not see it by chance.
She should ask how sampling variability and power could make eight cases look stronger than they are.
questions.explanation: Small samples can carry a vivid pattern while staying unstable. The warning travels beyond one profession because the mechanism is sampling noise.

questions.prompt: Lucas says, "The answer felt obvious as soon as I saw the first chart." What is the best response?
choices: The obvious feeling shows the example is strong enough without naming the mental step.
The obvious feeling is the target; ask which process made that bad inference feel easy.
The obvious feeling is mainly a summary problem, so the final claim needs a clearer slogan.
questions.explanation: The research target is the process that makes a weak inference feel plain. A slogan or vivid example skips the causal hinge.

questions.prompt: When Frances teaches a staff training, she wants to use the Israeli Air Force case without turning it into a generic expert story. What must stay in the lesson?
choices: The training must show how flight cadets, praise, and regression make feedback look causal.
The training can use any expert story if the staff remembers the emotional shape.
The training should center the instructor's forceful style because that is what people recall.
questions.explanation: The case is not a generic expert anecdote. Its force comes from cadet performance, praise, and natural variation doing the work.

questions.prompt: A hospital group quotes Paul Meehl, then keeps choosing forecasts by feel. Which change would make the example do real work?
choices: The group should score expert judgment beside an actuarial method before trusting the richer impression.
The group should repeat the flight-instructor lesson with new wording to make the same point.
The group should keep the Meehl story as background because biography gives the decision color.
questions.explanation: Meehl adds a second route: predictions should be scored, not merely felt. Biography alone does not change the decision rule.

questions.prompt: "Small samples are a lab issue," Levi says while reading a failed replication note for a training team. How should Iris answer without trapping the idea in one profession?
choices: She should keep the claim narrow because broad ideas do not need an institution to ground them.
She should point to Hebrew University, replication, and power to show how the pattern scales.
She should treat the failed replication as a local story until another profession repeats it.
questions.explanation: The small-sample case broadens the concept because a weak signal can fool careful research groups. Hebrew University and replication make that scope concrete.

questions.prompt: After a workshop on flight cadets and small samples, Miles says, "So the lesson is that people are irrational." Which reply keeps the harder claim intact?
choices: The slogan is safer because readers need a short warning before they can use statistics.
The stronger claim is that regression and sampling error clash with how experience feels.
The main lesson is that vivid cases should be distrusted whenever they involve experts.
questions.explanation: The hard edge rejects the broad insult. The useful claim names the specific statistical facts that make lived experience mislead.

reviewCards.front: How did the Israeli Air Force instructors misread praise and criticism?
reviewCards.back: They saw bad flights improve after criticism and good flights fall after praise. Regression to the mean could explain that swing without making criticism the cause.

reviewCards.front: What does regression to the mean ask you to check after an extreme result?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether the later result moved closer to the usual level on its own. A very high or low result can change next time without a new lesson working.

reviewCards.front: Why does Paul Meehl matter for expert prediction?
reviewCards.back: Meehl showed that global clinical judgment should face a scored comparison. A rich expert impression may feel wise and still predict worse than a simple rule.

reviewCards.front: Why can a small sample fool a careful researcher?
reviewCards.back: A few cases can line up by chance and feel stable. Statistical power and replication ask whether the pattern has enough data to survive another try.

reviewCards.front: What is the stronger lesson than "people are irrational"?
reviewCards.back: The stronger lesson names the missing fact. Regression and sampling error can clash with what experience feels like, so the mind tells a false causal story.

reviewCards.front: How would insider charisma (Ch 3) change the way you handle an error-pattern situation?
reviewCards.back: Use confidence to press the test, not to crown the story. Tversky-like force helps only when it drives a cleaner comparison between a vivid impression and a scored pattern.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice naming the pattern before you name the person. Ask whether the result was extreme, the sample was small, or the forecast was never scored. The skill is not doubt for its own sake. It is a short pause before praise, blame, or confidence hardens.

ifThenPlans.context: A result improves right after harsh feedback
ifThenPlans.plan: If a result improves after criticism, then write one sentence that tests regression first: "This may be a swing toward average, not proof the harsh words worked."

ifThenPlans.context: An expert forecast feels rich and humane
ifThenPlans.plan: If the story feels richer than the score, then ask for the rival prediction in plain words: "What would the simple rule forecast on this same case?"

ifThenPlans.context: A small group of cases looks surprisingly clean
ifThenPlans.plan: If a small sample looks decisive, then draft the caution before sharing it: "This pattern may shrink or vanish when we add cases."

ifThenPlans.context: You want to explain a mistake as foolishness
ifThenPlans.plan: If you reach for a character verdict, then replace it with a pattern question: "Which fact about regression, samples, or scoring did we miss?"

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, the first time a result feels obvious, pre-write the actual reply you will use. Compare two explanations in the words: "This may be skill" and "This may be noise."
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, tally each time you credit praise, blame, or a vivid expert story before checking the pattern. At week's end, read the number.

memorableLines.text: Variation can wear the mask of a lesson.
A score humbles a story.
Small samples can fake a loud signal.

chapters.title: The Collision
chapters.hook: Your first answer arrives wearing a lab coat, and you may never ask who dressed it.
chapters.counterintuition: The spark is not a meet-cute, but a method. A sharp clash over probability turned clean models into questions real experts could fail.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before one important response, draft one sentence naming the evidence that would make you change your mind.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When a tidy model feels too neat, turn the doubt into a testable question. The useful collision is the one that makes judgment visible.

breakdown.fastRead:
Layla marks 70:30 beside Ward Edwards's bookbag task and feels the answer settle too fast. If each poker chip sample points toward one bag, a formal Bayesian model tells her how belief should move. Edwards found a tidy pattern: people often moved in the right direction, but not far enough.

The collision begins when that tidy answer feels too generous. Clean tasks can hide messy minds. The useful doubt is not a sneer at math. It is a request for a sharper test. If even trained people lean on a small run of evidence as if it says more than it can, the problem is not ignorance. It is the way a live mind turns samples into confidence.
breakdown.deepRead:
A model can be useful and still be too polite about error. In Edwards's bookbag work, the poker chips made uncertainty clean. One bag held one mix, another held a different mix, and each draw gave fresh evidence. Bayesian updating means changing your odds as evidence arrives. Edwards's conservative Bayesian picture said people adjusted the right way, only with too much caution.

Desmond hears the snag while planning a seminar question. If the formal task is already so clean, what happens when the evidence is a short story, a vivid case, or a small study? A person may not update gently. He may leap. He may treat six cases like a crowd. A small sample can sound like a crowd.

That is why the Mathematical Psychology Association questionnaire mattered. The 1969 questions on sampling variability and statistical power were aimed at mathematically trained people. Statistical power means the chance a study can detect a real effect. Sampling variability means small samples bounce around more than large ones. If experts overtrust a small sample before any public action follows, the error sits inside planning itself.

The method is the real friendship engine here. One mind brings discomfort with the neat story. Another brings speed with formal models. Their talk turns a hunch into a question someone can answer wrong. A good argument makes a better instrument.
breakdown.fullRead:
Sawyer pays for the method before the meeting starts. He has a reply ready to a colleague who cites eight glowing user interviews. The old reply would be fast: eight is not enough. The new reply costs more. He has to ask what sample would count, what the eight cases can show, and which claim is still too large.

That cost is easy to miss in the origin story. The meeting is not useful because two gifted people happen to collide. It is useful because disagreement gets turned into a working device. Ward Edwards's 70:30 poker chips give one device. The 1969 questionnaire gives another. The 1971 Psychological Bulletin paper gives the error a name: the law of small numbers.

The law of small numbers is the false hope that a small sample will look like the larger world. The name is playful, but the damage is plain. A researcher plans a study with too few cases. A manager trusts the first six customer notes. A reader treats one neat example as proof. In each scene, the small pile feels more stable than it is.

Outsider sensitivity helps at the doorway. It makes Sawyer suspicious of confidence, including his own. But it can mislead if it stops there. Suspicion alone can become a mood. The next step is harder: make the doubt answerable. Write the question so a smart person can be surprised by the result.

Sawyer looks at the eight interviews again and notices two claims sitting on one line. One claim is modest: those eight people had a real complaint. The other claim is too large: the whole user base wants the same change. He can honor the first claim while shrinking the second. That is the useful discipline. It keeps vivid evidence in the room without letting it run the room.

There is a tradeoff. The method slows the room. It can make a clean answer feel less useful for a few minutes. Sawyer's colleague wants the reply now, not a lecture on samples. So Sawyer gives up the pleasure of sounding certain. He writes one sentence first: "What would we expect to see if eight interviews were only the loud edge of the larger group?" The sentence is slower than the verdict. It is also kinder to the decision.

The price of this idea is speed. You trade the quick comfort of a neat reading for a small test that may embarrass your first answer. That is not a small thing. In real work, the first answer often gets rewarded because it sounds ready. The harder gift is a habit of pausing before the answer hardens.

examples.title: Layla Crosses Out Bayes
examples.scenario: Layla crossed out the polite title, so the new seminar handout begins with Ward Edwards and a 70:30 poker-chip bookbag experiment. The expected story is neat: people see chips, update their odds, and fall a little short of Bayes. Then Layla writes the line that will break the room's guess: maybe the clean task flatters judgment before the real mess has even entered.
examples.whatToDo: Layla keeps the 70:30 bookbag on the first page, then adds a second prompt that asks where the formal model stops describing live judgment.
examples.whyItMatters: The reveal protects the model from becoming a lullaby. A clean setup can teach, but only if the next question tests what the setup leaves out.

examples.title: Desmond's Three Dots
examples.scenario: Desmond slides the question card under a motel-room phone at his desk the night before the 1969 Mathematical Psychology Association session. As the assistant shaping the packet, he keeps the program open beside him. Greta texts, "Too obvious?" Desmond types, "Only if training saves them." Greta: "Sampling variability first?" Desmond: "And power. If experts trust tiny studies, ignorance is not the culprit."
examples.whatToDo: Desmond trims the wording until the questionnaire tests one thing at a time: how much faith trained people place in small samples before results exist.
examples.whyItMatters: The thread shows the discipline under the spark. The plan is not to catch novices; it is to see whether expertise protects intuition when samples are small.

examples.title: Greta Restarts the Question
examples.scenario: The first draft is in the trash before Greta notices why her pulse has slowed. She had packed sampling variability, statistical power, and expert pride into one question for the Mathematical Psychology Association session. At the workshop bench, she stops sharpening the pencil. She starts again with one planned ask: how much can a small sample really promise?
examples.whatToDo: Greta pauses the routine, strips the draft to one sampling claim, and rehearses the cleaner question before any participant sees it.
examples.whyItMatters: The reset is the technique. A crowded test can hide the error it means to reveal, while one plain question lets the answer expose the assumption.

examples.title: Olivier Smells the Ink
examples.scenario: The paper smells faintly of ink, and Olivier rests one finger beside the phrase "law of small numbers" on the 1971 Psychological Bulletin proof. The desk is narrow. The margin is crowded. No one has acted on the paper yet. The small phrase does the work in advance: it makes the false faith in tiny samples easy to spot next time.
examples.whatToDo: Olivier checks that the title phrase points to the exact error: expecting a small sample to resemble the wider population too closely.
examples.whyItMatters: A good name carries a warning without turning into decoration. It helps the reader notice the same small-sample trap in a lab, memo, or reply.

examples.title: Julien Questions the Bag
examples.scenario: "Keep the bag in the question," Julien says, tapping the stack of Ward Edwards notes on the lake dock. "The 70:30 poker chips give us the clean case." Sawyer folds the corner of the page. "Then ask why real people do not feel like chips arriving one by one." Julien nods. "Do not throw Bayes away. Use it as the wall we can push against."
examples.whatToDo: Julien keeps Edwards's Bayesian updating model visible, then frames the next question around what the model cannot explain about everyday judgment.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange keeps the collision honest. The reader learns to challenge a model by testing its reach, not by sneering at its cleanest case.

examples.title: Craig Catches the Claim
examples.scenario: The pencil rolls off Craig's clipboard and drops between two boards on the front stoop. He bends for it and sees the sentence he just wrote: "These five interviews show what users want." The 1971 Psychological Bulletin phrase, the law of small numbers, catches him mid-draft. Five interviews can shape the next question. They cannot stand in for the whole user base.
examples.whatToDo: Craig replaces the broad claim with a narrower plan: use the five interviews to draft hypotheses, then state what larger sample would test them.
examples.whyItMatters: The recovery happens before the claim travels. Catching the overreach early keeps a small sample useful without letting it pretend to be the population.

questions.prompt: Layla sees the 70:30 bookbag task before a seminar. Which reading best fits Edwards's finding?
choices: The poker-chip story matters mainly because it is easy for readers to picture.
The task shows people ignore the evidence and choose from the first draw.
The task shows people update the right way, but less than Bayes would require.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 supports the third choice: Edwards treated people as conservative Bayesians. They moved with the evidence, but not far enough.

questions.prompt: "The formal model is mostly right; people only under-adjust." Which reading best catches what this response misses?
choices: It treats named researchers as enough support for the claim without checking the mechanism.
It assumes every formal model should be rejected once ordinary judgment looks messy.
It misses the doubt that everyday probability judgments follow even a partly correct Bayesian path.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 says the doubt was deeper than under-adjustment. The issue was whether everyday judgments follow that partly correct Bayesian process at all.

questions.prompt: Desmond sends the sampling questionnaire to mathematically trained participants. Which result would make the test matter most?
choices: It would add biographical color while leaving the decision lesson unchanged.
It would show that expert training does not keep intuition safe around sampling.
It would prove that untrained readers are the only group that mishandles probability.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 says the first joint questionnaire tested statistical intuitions among sophisticated participants. That makes expertise part of the test.

questions.prompt: A team trusts six cases because they look balanced across age, role, and mood. Which inference best names the error forming?
choices: They are treating the case as useful only inside the original research profession.
They are expecting a small sample to resemble the larger group too closely.
They are refusing to use a compact label for a repeated research problem.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 defines the law of small numbers as the false expectation that small samples closely resemble the population.

questions.prompt: Two colleagues keep arguing before they write the study question. Which response best names the useful result that can follow?
choices: Their conversation can become the lab where intuitions are turned into testable problems.
Their conversation can stay a lively summary without needing a concrete condition.
Their conversation can replace the need to test the intuition with outside answers.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 says the collaboration worked because conversation itself became the lab where intuitions turned into problems.

questions.prompt: "Any expert anecdote could open the opening lesson." Which response best preserves the source case?
choices: A vivid expert story can work if it makes the opening easier to remember.
A different expert story can work if the later lesson names probability.
The 70:30 bookbag task matters because it is the formal target being tested.
questions.explanation: Fact 6 anchors the scene in Ward Edwards's 70:30 bookbag task. It is not interchangeable because it supplies the formal mechanism.

questions.prompt: Greta adds the 1969 questionnaire after the bookbag scene. Which reading best explains what the second case adds?
choices: It shows that mathematical expertise still may not protect intuition from sampling error.
It repeats the same case in new words so the reader sees the point twice.
It proves that formal training is useless whenever people face uncertainty.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 says the questionnaire adds a second check: expertise in mathematics does not immunize intuition against sampling error.

questions.prompt: Olivier sees "law of small numbers" in the Psychological Bulletin proof. Which inference best explains why the label matters?
choices: It turns a recurring error into a research object that can travel beyond one person.
It lets a broad claim stand without naming any concrete institution or publication.
It makes the paper memorable even if the mechanism stays inside the original scene.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 says the law of small numbers broadened the concept because a label turned the recurring error into a research object.

questions.prompt: A reader calls the collision a story about two brilliant minds meeting. Which reading best names what the reader flattened?
choices: The reader has made the source material safer by turning it into a simple slogan.
The reader has missed that disagreement about a model produced testable questions.
The reader has kept the meeting focused by leaving out the method behind it.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 gives the hard edge: the meeting is not a simple origin myth. Its mechanism is disagreement becoming testable questions.

reviewCards.front: What did Ward Edwards's 70:30 bookbag task make clean enough to test?
reviewCards.back: It made Bayesian updating visible. People saw poker-chip evidence and moved their odds in the right direction, but not as far as the formal rule required.

reviewCards.front: What is the law of small numbers warning you not to trust?
reviewCards.back: Do not trust a tiny sample to look like the wider group. A few vivid cases can help form a question, but they cannot carry the weight of a population.

reviewCards.front: Why did the Mathematical Psychology Association questionnaire aim at trained participants?
reviewCards.back: The target mattered because math skill was not the shield being assumed. If trained people still overtrusted small samples, the error was inside intuition, not just ignorance.

reviewCards.front: Where does outsider sensitivity (Ch 2) help here, and where would leaning on it mislead you?
reviewCards.back: It helps you distrust a confident first read. It misleads if it stops at suspicion, because the collision asks you to turn doubt into a clear question someone can answer.

reviewCards.front: How can a conversation become more than talk in the collision?
reviewCards.back: It becomes useful when each intuition is shaped into a problem. The test is whether the exchange produces a question that can expose a wrong answer.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice turning a neat first answer into one testable question. Use the One-Rehearsal Test: before you reply, say one sentence that names what evidence would change your mind. This keeps doubt practical instead of vague.

ifThenPlans.context: When a clean model makes the answer feel finished
ifThenPlans.plan: If the model settles the room too fast, then run the One-Rehearsal Test and ask where real judgment may stop matching the model.

ifThenPlans.context: When a few vivid cases feel like enough
ifThenPlans.plan: If six notes or five interviews sound like the whole story, then run the One-Rehearsal Test and name the larger group they might not represent.

ifThenPlans.context: When expertise makes a sampling claim sound safe
ifThenPlans.plan: If a trained person trusts a small sample, then run the One-Rehearsal Test and ask what sample size would make the claim stronger.

ifThenPlans.context: When a disagreement starts to become personal
ifThenPlans.plan: If the clash turns into status, then run the One-Rehearsal Test and restate the dispute as a question that evidence could answer.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For one day, when your fingers reach the keyboard for an important response, draft one sentence: what evidence would make your current answer weaker?
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, swap your usual instant reply for the One-Rehearsal Test in the first half, then reply normally in the second half. Compare which half caught more overclaiming.

chapters.title: The Mind's Rules
chapters.hook: 3 blank answer lines looked neutral, while the first number quietly tugged the pencil.
chapters.counterintuition: Useful shortcuts, repeatable mistakes: the same rule that saves work can swap a hard question for an easier one.
chapters.tryThisNow: The next time you feel the pull to trust a fast answer, write it once, count 3 cues that made it feel easy, then name the rule steering it.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Fast judgment gets safer when you ask which rule is working: similarity, easy recall, or a starting number that has pulled the answer toward itself.

breakdown.fastRead:
A mixed stack of profile sheets sits on the table. Some are from engineers, some from lawyers, and one thin sketch sounds like a quiet tinkerer. Brett wants to call him an engineer. Trent points to the base rates first. If the count leans one way, the sketch has to fight that count. Fast answers often arrive wearing the face of sight.

The mind uses rules to save effort. A heuristic is a quick rule of thumb, a way to answer under fog. The danger is not that the rule fails each time. A shortcut survives because it often helps. The danger is the quiet swap. Similarity stands in for probability. Easy memory stands in for frequency. A first number stands in for the whole estimate.

Check the rule before you trust the result.
breakdown.deepRead:
A small rule can feel like a fact. When Brett sees the engineer-like profile, his mind is not doing nothing. It is matching a sketch to a type. That move is representativeness: judging by how much one thing resembles a pattern. It can help when the pattern is real. It misleads when the known count, the base rate, gets shoved aside.

Brooke feels the same pull on a word list. Asked whether more words begin with the letter K or have K in the third position, she can summon key, kite, and kitchen fast. Third-position words sit deeper in memory. They are harder to fetch, so the smaller pile feels larger. That is availability. Memory hands her a sample, and she mistakes the sample for the world.

Anchoring works through a different door. Ludovic hears an arbitrary number before making a numeric estimate. He knows the number should not matter. Still, his answer leans toward it. Adjustment starts from the anchor and stops too soon. The first number becomes a hidden mark on the page.

These rules are not sins. They are tools with weak spots. You cannot inspect every count, memory sample, and estimate from scratch all day. You can pause when the answer feels too smooth. Smooth is a clue, not a verdict. Ask what the mind just used as evidence.
breakdown.fullRead:
Brooke's pencil stops over the letter K. The question looks childish, almost like a warm-up. Which is more common: words that start with K, or words where K sits after two earlier letters? Her head fills with crisp starts. Kettle. Kind. Keep. The other group is harder to search, so it seems smaller. The error is not laziness. It is a bad sample wearing a clean shirt.

That is why the work matters. The research did not collect odd mistakes for sport. It named rules that produce families of mistakes. Representativeness makes the engineer-lawyer problem feel obvious because a profile resembles a type. Availability makes the K task feel obvious because memory gives some words faster than others. Anchoring makes a numeric estimate feel reasoned even when an arbitrary number set the first step.

Trent's better answer to Brett is not, "Never trust the profile." The profile may carry information. His better answer is, "Start with the base rates, then let the profile earn its weight." That order matters. If the story gets first chair, the count becomes an afterthought. If the count speaks first, the story has to add evidence instead of replacing it.

Teagan gives Tyler the same reframe in a hallway after a training quiz. "A rule of mind is not a flaw; it is a tool that needs a guardrail." Tyler had wanted to fix each wrong answer one by one. Teagan points to the pattern. One guardrail checks the count behind a similar story. One checks whether memory had a fair chance to search. One checks whether the first number deserves power.

A guardrail can be light. Brett writes one count in the margin. Brooke asks for one slower search. Ludovic makes one clean estimate before the displayed number appears. None of them becomes a full-time skeptic. Each person gives the fast rule a small check at the spot where it tends to bend.

Madeleine learns the hard part while drafting an estimate sheet. If she asks for a number after showing a prior figure, she may have planted an anchor. If she asks for a guess before the cue, the estimate has a cleaner start. The same person can look more or less wise because the question changed shape.

When should you do the opposite? When speed matters more than accuracy, and the cost of checking is higher than the cost of being a little wrong. You do not need a base-rate audit to choose soup at lunch. You do need one when hiring, pricing, diagnosing, forecasting, or judging how often something happens. Identify the shortcut, then ask whether the moment deserves the slower answer.

examples.title: The Profile Pile
examples.scenario: 2 job labels. That is the split Brett and Trent face at the source-case profile table: engineer or lawyer. Brett reads the engineer-lawyer problem by feel. The shy tinkerer sounds like an engineer, so his probability judgment jumps. Trent starts with the base rates and lets the profile add only a little. Brett lands on the vivid match. Trent lands closer to the count.
examples.whatToDo: Trent writes the base rates at the top of the sheet before reading the profile again. Brett rereads the same sketch and marks which details are only representativeness cues.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast shows why similarity feels like evidence. A profile can still matter, but it should not erase the count that came with the engineer-lawyer problem.

examples.title: Tyler's K List
examples.scenario: After choosing the K-start column, Learner Tyler keeps his pencil moving down the afternoon training-room worksheet. Teagan stops beside the doorway and asks him to name three words with K in the third position. He stalls. "Easy to fetch is not the same as often true," Teagan says. The availability heuristic has made the word-frequency judgment feel settled.
examples.whatToDo: Tyler writes two sample lists side by side, then marks which list was easier to search. He treats recall speed as a clue about memory, not a count of the world.
examples.whyItMatters: The coach talk gives the reader a portable sentence. When examples rush forward, the first question is whether memory had a fair way to search.

examples.title: Brooke Finds the Third Slot
examples.scenario: Sliding the worksheet across the classroom desk, student Brooke taps the blank for the third position and frowns. The class has filled the board with letter K starters, but the hidden category is larger. Brooke's confusion becomes the lesson: the availability heuristic makes a word-frequency judgment lean toward the pile memory can reach first.
examples.whatToDo: Teagan has Brooke sort found words by K at the start and K in the third position. Brooke counts both piles only after seeing how uneven recall felt.
examples.whyItMatters: A school case makes the mechanism visible. The wrong answer is not a lack of care; it is the feel of an easy search being mistaken for evidence.

examples.title: Ludovic's Second Estimate
examples.scenario: The answer sheet on the estimate-room desk shows two numeric estimates where participant Ludovic expected one. Earlier, before the wheel, he wrote a low guess and shrugged. Later, after an arbitrary number appeared, his second answer climbed. He knows about anchoring and still makes an insufficient adjustment. The changed variable is only the starting number.
examples.whatToDo: Ludovic writes his first estimate before seeing any cue, then compares it with the later anchored estimate. He circles the shift instead of defending it.
examples.whyItMatters: The before-and-after view catches anchoring in motion. Knowing a number is arbitrary does not stop it from becoming a starting point.

examples.title: The Buzzing Number
examples.scenario: The phone buzzes on the metal table, and the displayed number steals Madeleine's eyes before the estimate sheet opens. "That value is arbitrary," she says. Ludovic nods. "Then why did your numeric estimate move toward it?" "Because adjustment started there." "So the question planted anchoring before the answer began."
examples.whatToDo: Madeleine moves the prior number below the estimate box and asks for the first guess before any cue appears. Ludovic checks whether adjustment still starts from the old value.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange keeps the lesson small and testable. A number can guide judgment even when both people agree it should have no claim.

examples.title: Teagan's Quiet Check
examples.scenario: "Pick the likely profession," the instruction says, and Teagan feels the engineer answer rise before she has read the base rates twice. No talking. The engineer-lawyer problem is doing its trick. Similarity feels clean. Probability judgment needs the dull count. She writes the count first, then lets representativeness argue second.
examples.whatToDo: Teagan slows the private answer by naming the two inputs: base rates first, profile fit second. She lets the profile revise the count instead of replacing it.
examples.whyItMatters: The inner monologue shows the repair where the error starts. A heuristic often appears as the answer, so the check has to happen before confidence hardens.

questions.prompt: During the profile exercise, Brett chooses engineer from the sketch before weighing the known mix of jobs. What is missing from his answer?
choices: Similarity is pulling the probability estimate away from the base rates.
The vivid profile supplies the missing count for the whole sample.
The profile should be ignored because stories have no judgment value.
questions.explanation: Representativeness judges by similarity. The engineer-like sketch may matter, but the probability judgment still has to start with the base rates.

questions.prompt: Brooke fills a worksheet with K-starting words, then struggles to find words with K in the third position. Which reading fits the task?
choices: The named words make the K-starting category the better count.
The harder search means third-position words are too rare to matter.
Ease of recall is standing in for the word-frequency judgment.
questions.explanation: Availability makes easy examples feel more frequent. Brooke's memory sample is not the same as the true word-frequency count.

questions.prompt: A wheel lands on a high number before Ludovic gives a numeric estimate. His answer stays high after he adjusts. What happened?
choices: The wheel supplied a useful biography clue for the estimate.
The arbitrary number became an anchor, and adjustment stopped too soon.
The later estimate escaped the first value because Ludovic knew it was random.
questions.explanation: Anchoring makes estimates cling to a starting value. Even an arbitrary number can pull the answer when adjustment is not enough.

questions.prompt: After the K task and the anchor task mislead classmates, Tyler wants to ban every shortcut. Which reply best fits the hard edge?
choices: Heuristics conserve effort and often work well enough to survive.
Heuristics persist because they are usually accurate enough to ignore.
Heuristics belong only to old lab tasks and do not travel elsewhere.
questions.explanation: The rules persist because they reduce effort and often help. Their errors matter because the same useful rule can fail in patterned ways.

questions.prompt: After three lab tasks produce different wrong answers, a reader treats each one as a separate slip. Which next step matches the research program?
choices: File each slip as a one-time lapse with no shared cause.
Replace the experiments with a list of memorable stories.
Look for mental rules that produce families of mistakes.
questions.explanation: The shift was from isolated errors to rules that generate patterns. Representativeness, availability, and anchoring each create a family of mistakes.

questions.prompt: Someone swaps the engineer-lawyer problem for any expert anecdote with a vivid ending. What has been lost?
choices: The anecdote still works because any expert story can test probability.
The base-rate setting that shows similarity overpowering known counts.
The profile detail that proves all base rates should be discarded.
questions.explanation: The engineer-lawyer problem is not a generic expert tale. It tests how representativeness can push probability judgment away from base rates.

questions.prompt: During a word-frequency exercise, a list feels settled because the first examples come quickly. Which check best uses the K-letter task?
choices: Ask whether memory fluency is impersonating statistical evidence.
Ask whether the same profile can be used with new profession names.
Ask whether the first number on the page deserves more weight.
questions.explanation: The K-letter task adds a route distinct from base rates and anchors. It shows how memory fluency can impersonate evidence about frequency.

questions.prompt: A pricing team sees last year's figure before making this year's estimate. Which concern follows from anchoring demonstrations?
choices: The old figure is broad enough that no concrete estimate is needed.
The old figure may become a hidden coordinate system for the new estimate.
The old figure can serve as context without biasing the new estimate.
questions.explanation: Anchoring broadens the concept beyond one person. An irrelevant or stale starting point can still shape the team's numeric estimate.

questions.prompt: At the end of the workshop, Tyler says, "Heuristic means defect, so the cure is to distrust every shortcut." How should that claim be revised?
choices: A simpler slogan is safer because it keeps readers away from all quick rules.
Shortcuts should be praised because a useful rule does not create errors.
Shortcuts can be efficient enough to keep and patterned enough to correct.
questions.explanation: The hard edge is dual. Heuristics are not pure defects, but their errors are systematic enough to name, study, and guard against.

reviewCards.front: What is a heuristic in plain words?
reviewCards.back: A heuristic is a quick rule of thumb the mind uses under uncertainty. It helps save effort, but it can swap the hard question for one that feels easier.

reviewCards.front: How does representativeness bend the engineer-lawyer task?
reviewCards.back: It lets a profile's similarity to an engineer or lawyer feel like probability. The repair is to start with the base rates, then let the description add evidence.

reviewCards.front: Why does the K-letter task fool many careful readers?
reviewCards.back: Words beginning with K come to mind more easily than words with K in the third position. Availability turns recall speed into a false cue about frequency.

reviewCards.front: What is the anchoring warning for numeric estimates?
reviewCards.back: A first number can become the place adjustment starts, even when the number is arbitrary. The later answer often stays too close to that starting point.

reviewCards.front: Why is it wrong to treat heuristics as pure defects?
reviewCards.back: They survive because they often work and save effort. The real lesson is to keep the useful shortcut while adding checks where its errors are patterned.

reviewCards.front: How does insider charisma (Ch 3) connect to checking a fast mental rule?
reviewCards.back: Insider charisma can make confidence feel like proof. Ask which rule produced that confidence: similarity, easy recall, or an anchor.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice naming the quick rule before you accept the answer. Ask whether the pull came from similarity, easy recall, or a starting number. The skill is not distrust; it is knowing when a fast answer deserves a guardrail.

ifThenPlans.context: If a profile sounds like an obvious type in a hiring or scoring choice,
ifThenPlans.plan: then write the base rates first and let the story change them only after it adds real evidence.

ifThenPlans.context: If examples arrive fast and make a risk feel common,
ifThenPlans.plan: then ask whether availability gave you a fair memory sample or only the easiest cases.

ifThenPlans.context: If a prior number appears before your estimate,
ifThenPlans.plan: then make a clean first estimate on a separate line before adjusting from the shown number.

ifThenPlans.context: If you want to reject a shortcut just because it can err,
ifThenPlans.plan: then name where it helps and where it needs a check.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next day, stage one fast-judgment moment once: write the fast answer, label the likely rule, and add one check before acting.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Teach the Rule Check to one person this week in your own words. Use the engineer-lawyer base rates, the K-letter task, and anchoring as the three examples.

A shortcut survives because it often helps.
