chapters.title: The Rules of Prediction
chapters.hook: When I trust one vivid case, how far should I move my forecast?
chapters.counterintuition: What looks like bland caution is actually respect for evidence: start with the class, then move only as far as the case earns.
chapters.tryThisNow: At your next handoff between tasks, place a 3-minute calendar block named Shrink the Forecast. Count six slow breaths, write the base rate, then adjust one prediction.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Strong impressions can help prediction, but only after you start with the class, check validity, and pull extreme forecasts toward the average.

breakdown.fastRead: Myriam watches an IDF officer candidate shine during a field test. His voice is clear, his group follows, and the leadership rating on the form begs for a high forecast. The old move is to let that one scene carry the future. Prediction discipline asks for a slower move: start with the base rate, ask how valid the evidence is, then move partway. A vivid case is not a whole class. Strong evidence matters, but noisy evidence should not make a wild forecast.
breakdown.deepRead:
A forecast goes wrong when the case feels cleaner than it is. In the 1973 Psychological Review paper, representativeness made people treat a good fit as a good prediction. A student sounds like an engineer, so the mind jumps toward engineer. A candidate looks like a leader, so the mind jumps toward command. The jump feels like seeing, but it is still a bet.

Brian has a stack of IDF candidate ratings and one sheet near the top looks almost too easy. The candidate spoke first, solved the map problem, and pulled quiet teammates into the task. Brian wants to write star officer beside the score. Then he checks the class. How many candidates with great field moments later became strong officers? How much do these ratings usually predict? That pause changes the number. Extreme evidence still needs a leash.

Regression toward the mean is the plain reason. When one event is far above the usual level, the next event often falls closer to average. Not because the first event was fake. It may have been real. But luck, mood, task fit, and measurement error helped make it extreme. If those forces do not repeat, the next result will look less dramatic. The rule is not cold. It keeps one bright performance from becoming a prophecy.
breakdown.fullRead:
Jean's pen hovers over the lower forecast, and the discomfort is not mathematical. A rule that shrinks a prediction can feel like an insult to the person in front of you. Jean sees a candidate calm a tense group, and the lower forecast feels unfair. She watched the act. She heard the voice steady. She saw men move because he moved first. A base rate can seem thin beside that.

A 1973 Psychological Review page gives Jean a way to keep the scene without obeying it. If leadership ratings have only modest validity, they can move the forecast, but not all the way to the edge. The case gets a vote. The class gets a vote too. Rules protect judgment from its own confidence.

A file can hold a life story, a test score, an interview note, and a trained observer's hunch. That richness has value. It can also hide the fact that no one has checked how well the hunch predicts later outcomes. Scored rules can embarrass confident experts because they make error visible. They ask, after the fact, whose forecasts worked.

Yves learns the lesson at a reception desk, where a caller wants a fast answer about a new applicant. The file has one glowing reference and one thin work sample. The vivid reference pulls his mind toward a bold forecast. The work sample pulls less hard because it is dull. Yves writes the base rate first: most applicants with this profile perform near the middle. Then he lets the reference move the forecast a little, not a mile.

A rain app can teach calibration faster than a lecture. Calibration means matching confidence to the quality of the evidence. If a rain forecast says 70 percent on ten similar days, rain should come on about seven of them. If a leadership forecast says high potential, the later record should back that level of confidence across many people. One forecast can be lucky. A set of forecasts tells the truth.

On Beckett's form, three questions sit above the final number. What class does this case belong to? How often does this class produce the outcome? How valid is the case evidence for that outcome? Prediction discipline does not say individual facts are useless. It says those facts need to pass through the questions before they rule the forecast. Without them, a story can smuggle in certainty.

Delphine can misuse the rule when her job is to help one person grow. Working one on one with a nervous candidate, she should not treat him as an average before every drill. Training needs attention to the person. Prediction needs the class. The error comes when a coach's close care is borrowed for a forecast about the future. Care can be personal; prediction must be checked.

examples.title: Folder With Two Pulls
examples.scenario: The folder has one bright score and one dull number. Myriam holds the IDF officer candidates sheet after a field exercise where leadership ratings crowned one recruit. She must decide between two bad calls: crown a lucky hour as destiny or flatten a real leader. The base rate in the margin makes both choices costly.
examples.whatToDo: Myriam keeps the high observation in the file, writes the base rate beside it, and moves the forecast partway instead of all the way.
examples.whyItMatters: The move protects both sides of judgment. The vivid case still counts, but noisy evidence no longer gets to speak as if it were a full career.

examples.title: Date on the Proof
examples.scenario: 1973. Brian taps the year on the Psychological Review proof while Delphine reads beside the editorial desk. "The strong fit sounds like a strong forecast," Delphine says. Brian points to the word representativeness. "Only if the fit predicts well." Delphine turns the page. "So the match is evidence." Brian nods. "Evidence with a weight, not a crown."
examples.whatToDo: Brian keeps the description on the page, then asks Delphine to mark how valid that kind of description has been before trusting its pull.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange keeps the paper practical. A description can be useful and still too weak to justify the extreme forecast it makes tempting.

examples.title: Star Score Shrinks
examples.scenario: Jean has sent the recruit's command forecast up the chain, so the next page ought to confirm it. The IDF officer candidates ledger shows top leadership ratings from the field exercise. Then the follow-up line arrives: solid, not exceptional. The first score had not lied. Regression had pulled the next measure toward the middle.
examples.whatToDo: Jean keeps the first rating as evidence, then lowers the forecast around regression instead of treating the later average result as a betrayal.
examples.whyItMatters: The reveal teaches the forecast rule in one body blow. Extreme first signals often soften later, even when the first signal was real.

examples.title: Text Before the Bet
examples.scenario:
Yves thumbs a reply at the reception desk before the final sentence is even typed.
Yves: The case screams success.
Delphine: What class is it in?
Yves: Small sample, strong match.
Delphine: 1973 Psychological Review problem: representativeness.
Yves: Base rate first?
Delphine: Base rate, then validity, then prediction.
Yves deletes the word certain.
examples.whatToDo: Yves leaves the vivid case in the note, but he puts the reference class and validity check before the final forecast sentence.
examples.whyItMatters: The thread makes the pause small enough to use. One good question can stop a clean story from becoming a claim the evidence cannot support.

examples.title: Rank List Reset
examples.scenario: The base-rate column is blank when the shortlist reaches Beckett's hand. The IDF officer candidates names sit in neat order, with leadership ratings doing all the work. Beckett caps the pen, slides the page back to the top of the pile, and restarts the review with regression written in the margin.
examples.whatToDo: Beckett stops the ranking routine, writes the class average at the top, and scores each candidate's evidence against that starting point.
examples.whyItMatters: The reset turns calibration into a habit. The pause is not delay; it is the moment the forecast gets an anchor that belongs there.

examples.title: Pencil Under Validity
examples.scenario: The pencil rasps under the word validity, and Delphine hears the small sound twice. The Psychological Review page is thin enough for the desk grain to show through. Beside prediction, she writes class, weight, error. The room does not change. The forecast does: the same case now has a measured pull.
examples.whatToDo: Delphine turns the marked word into three plain checks: name the class, weigh the evidence, and leave room for error in the forecast.
examples.whyItMatters: The small note makes the abstract rule usable. Validity becomes a question about how hard this evidence should be allowed to pull.

questions.prompt: Myriam reads a one-page profile that fits the image of a future leader almost perfectly. Before she changes the forecast, which next move best follows prediction discipline?
choices: She should treat the clean fit as enough proof to make the forecast bold.
She should ask for another vivid profile before touching the starting estimate.
She should check how reliable that kind of profile is before moving far.
questions.explanation: Representativeness makes the clean fit feel stronger than it is. The profile can move the forecast, but only after Myriam asks how well such profiles predict.

questions.prompt: "That candidate was outstanding today, so the next report should be outstanding too." Which reply best catches the prediction error in Brian's claim?
choices: Today's rating is useful only if Brian removes the candidate from the usual class.
Today's rating should be replaced by a fresh interview before any forecast is made.
Today's rating may be real, yet the next result should often sit closer to average.
questions.explanation: Regression does not call the first rating fake. It says an extreme result often includes noise, so later evidence often lands nearer the middle.

questions.prompt: A selection board hears one vivid account of an IDF candidate and starts ignoring the usual outcomes for similar candidates. Which correction belongs first?
choices: Start with the reference class, then let the vivid account adjust it.
Let the vivid account define the class because it contains the freshest detail.
Set the class aside until the board has a second story about the candidate.
questions.explanation: Base rates supply the class the story tries to displace. The story still matters, but it should adjust a starting point instead of replacing it.

questions.prompt: At the rating table, Myriam says, "I've watched enough candidates to know when leadership is real." What does she miss if she stops there?
choices: Her experience still needs a rule that tempers strong impressions.
Her experience should be ignored whenever the candidate looked impressive.
Her experience works best when no one scores the later results.
questions.explanation: Expertise can notice real cues, but sincerity and practice do not fix prediction error by themselves. Myriam needs a rule for weighting the cue.

questions.prompt: Fabrice's office prizes detailed case notes and dislikes scored forecasts. If the research threatens that office, what is the pressure point?
choices: Detailed notes may take longer to write than a scored forecast.
Scored forecasts can show when confident case judgment misses.
Case judgment may use richer language than a simple rule allows.
questions.explanation: The threat is not that case notes are short or cold. Scoring makes error visible, and that changes the status of untested confidence.

questions.prompt: A draft replaces On the Psychology of Prediction with a generic story about an expert making a bad call. Which loss matters most?
choices: The draft loses the link between representativeness and imperfect validity.
The draft gains a broader setting but keeps the same prediction mechanism.
The draft makes the expert easier to picture than the paper's test.
questions.explanation: The paper anchors a precise mechanism: a good fit can feel too predictive. A generic expert story may be vivid while losing that testable link.

questions.prompt: When the IDF candidate ratings enter the discussion after the paper, what should a reader expect them to add?
choices: They should repeat the paper's point with a new label for the same evidence.
They should replace the paper because field ratings matter more than concepts.
They should show how noisy evidence changes a real leadership forecast.
questions.explanation: The IDF case is not a repeat with new scenery. It gives a field check on noisy evidence, base rates, and regression in leadership ratings.

questions.prompt: A professional group says its forecasts are too personal to score. Which answer best applies the lesson at institutional scale?
choices: Personal detail should be removed so every forecast uses the same words.
Scoring can test whether confident judgment predicts outcomes at scale.
Professional status should decide which forecasts count as valid evidence.
questions.explanation: The broader lesson is about answerable confidence. Scoring predictions tests whether expert judgment works across cases, not just in one rich file.

questions.prompt: During a forecast review, Beckett says, "The safest forecast is to ignore the individual case and trust the average." What is wrong with that shortcut?
choices: It treats vivid individual evidence as stronger than any class evidence.
It drops useful case evidence instead of calibrating it with the class.
It treats calibration as a way to avoid checking later forecast errors.
questions.explanation: The hard edge is calibration, not distrust. Keep useful case detail, then weigh it against the class and the evidence's track record.

reviewCards.front: What is prediction discipline trying to slow down?
reviewCards.back: It slows the jump from a vivid case to an extreme forecast. The pause makes you name the class, check how valid the evidence is, and leave room for error.

reviewCards.front: Why does regression make a brilliant first signal risky to overread?
reviewCards.back: A brilliant first signal can be real and still include luck, task fit, and noise. Later results often move closer to average when those extra forces fade.

reviewCards.front: What job does a base rate do before a vivid story takes over?
reviewCards.back: A base rate names the class and its usual outcome. It gives the forecast a starting point, so the vivid story adjusts the number instead of replacing it.

reviewCards.front: What does heuristics as rules of mind (Ch 6) get WRONG if you applied it naively to IDF candidate ratings?
reviewCards.back: It might stop at spotting representativeness. Prediction needs the next step: decide how much that cue should move the forecast after base rates and validity are known.

reviewCards.front: Why is expert sincerity not enough to fix prediction error?
reviewCards.back: A sincere expert can still overweight the case in front of them. A rule for tempering impressions makes the forecast answerable to error instead of confidence.

reviewCards.front: What false shortcut should prediction discipline reject about individual evidence?
reviewCards.back: The false shortcut is to distrust every case detail. Calibration keeps the detail, weighs it against the class, and moves only as far as validity allows.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice shrinking a forecast before it hardens. Start with the class, ask how well this kind of evidence predicts, then move only partway from the base rate. The move protects a vivid case from becoming a prophecy. It lets strong evidence count without letting it take over.

ifThenPlans.context: If a story about one person feels like enough to settle the forecast
ifThenPlans.plan: If one story starts to settle the forecast, then run Shrink the Forecast First by writing the reference class before the case detail.

ifThenPlans.context: If a result sits far above or below the usual range
ifThenPlans.plan: If one result is extreme, then run Shrink the Forecast First by asking what would happen if the next result moved toward average.

ifThenPlans.context: If confidence rises because the observer has seen many cases
ifThenPlans.plan: If expertise starts to feel like proof, then run Shrink the Forecast First by asking what rule keeps the impression from running too far.

ifThenPlans.context: If someone says the average is all that matters
ifThenPlans.plan: If the class starts erasing the person, then run Shrink the Forecast First by letting valid case evidence move the forecast a measured amount.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: During the next 24 hours, use a timer or calendar block at your next transition between tasks. Count six breaths, name one base rate, then shrink one forecast before acting on it.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Use spaced reps three times this week. At the first task handoff, shrink a low-stakes forecast. Two days later, shrink a people forecast. Near week's end, shrink a high-stakes forecast and write what changed.

memorableLines.text: A vivid case is not a whole class.
Extreme evidence still needs a leash.
Rules protect judgment from its own confidence.

chapters.title: Going Viral
chapters.hook: The hospital chart looked settled, but the missed clue was hiding in the first label.
chapters.counterintuition: Expert judgment can save lives and still need a guardrail. The danger is not stupidity; it is a smart person trusting the first clean story too soon.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before you start your next judgment call, spend ten minutes writing one line: "The first story pulling me is ___."
chapters.keyTakeaway: Kahneman and Tversky's ideas went viral because they helped experts catch predictable errors before a vivid case or early label hardened into judgment.

breakdown.fastRead:
Donald Redelmeier gives the idea its door into real life. In internal medicine, a patient does not arrive as a puzzle in a textbook. A triage label, a recent case, and a doctor's first hunch can steer what gets noticed next. Expert hands can still miss a predictable bend in thought.

That is why the work left psychology. A vivid case can crowd out the quiet base rate. A first label can become an anchor. Expertise needs backup when the first story feels too easy.
breakdown.deepRead:
The mechanism is simple enough to see on a hospital floor. Availability means a recent or vivid case comes to mind fast. Anchoring means the first label keeps pulling later evidence toward it. Representativeness means the patient seems to fit a familiar pattern, so missing facts get less weight.

Redelmeier helped carry those ideas into medical decision-making in Toronto. The lesson was not that doctors were careless. It was that trained people also judge under uncertainty. A doctor who saw one dramatic diagnosis last week may see its shadow in today's patient. A chart that starts with one early label may make every lab result look like support. Risk gets real when someone else pays for your shortcut.

Cass Sunstein and Richard Thaler show the second route. The same research gave law, behavioral economics, and government regulation a new model of people. Policy did not need to assume calm, perfect choosers. It could be built around common human errors. A check is not an insult; it is a handrail.
breakdown.fullRead:
Wallace's counter-case is a patient whose symptoms truly fit the first label. The senior doctor does not need a long bias ritual before ordering the obvious treatment. Delay would be the error. The rule is not to distrust every expert hunch. It is to know when a hunch has started editing the evidence.

That boundary matters because the research could be misread as a war on expertise. Redelmeier's medical work points the other way. Internal medicine needs trained judgment because patients are complex and time matters. The backup is for the places where training can make a shortcut feel more certain than it is. A checklist, a second look, or a base-rate question protects the patient from premature closure.

Evidence-based medicine made the same point at a wider scale. Evidence-based means using the best available research to check care, not treating a doctor like a clerk. The practice asks for a link between what is done and what is known. It gives the vivid story less power when the broader record says caution.

That shift changes the moral feel of error. A wrong call is no longer only a private lapse by one doctor, judge, or analyst. Once a common bias has a name and a routine can catch it, the institution owns part of the repair. A ward can ask for a second look. A regulator can test a default. A manager can slow a decision when the opening story is too neat.

Sunstein and Thaler took the spread into law and policy. Their interest in Kahneman and Tversky was practical: if people predict, choose, and remember in patterned ways, institutions can be designed with those patterns in mind. Behavioral economics matters because public errors are not random dust. They repeat. Forms, rules, and defaults can either ignore that fact or make room for it.

The title is apt, but the spread was not viral because the idea sounded clever. It traveled because doctors, lawyers, economists, regulators, and managers saw their own work in it. These were not classroom tricks anymore. They were mistakes with patients, clients, markets, and citizens on the far end.

The counter-case keeps the idea honest. If a patient is crashing and the evidence cleanly points one way, the right move may be swift expert action. Obeying the bias check as a ritual would then be a mistake. But when the room is calm enough for one more question, ask it: what early label, vivid memory, or familiar pattern is doing quiet work here? The best expertise does not fear that question. It uses it before certainty gets too comfortable.

examples.title: Triage Label Turn
examples.scenario: The triage sticker curls at the edge of the chart while Wallace presents the case on a Toronto internal medicine round. He hears himself treating the first label as if Donald Redelmeier's warning were only for other doctors. Mid-sentence, Wallace stops. The lab result he had called noise may be the clue, and the patient deserves a second pass before the label hardens.
examples.whatToDo: Wallace names the early label aloud, then rereads the chart for facts it made easy to ignore. He corrects the error while the team can still change course.
examples.whyItMatters: The useful moment is not looking flawless. It is noticing when expertise has started defending its first story and reopening the evidence before care narrows.

examples.title: Memo With Handrails
examples.scenario: Every option in the draft assumed citizens would read, compare, and choose with calm attention. Tristan wrote the next paragraph as a memo: "Cass Sunstein and Richard Thaler treat Kahneman and Tversky as a warning for regulation. If people make patterned errors, the form should guide choices instead of pretending friction is neutral."
examples.whatToDo: Tristan revises the draft so the public form uses plain defaults and checks. The memo turns behavioral economics into a design test, not a lecture.
examples.whyItMatters: A lab finding matters in policy when it changes the shape of a form or rule. The idea leaves psychology by becoming part of public design.

examples.title: Three Chart Paths
examples.scenario: Three charts sit open at 8 a.m. in a teaching clinic's evidence-based medicine seminar on decision science. Manon starts with the case that looks most like last week's diagnosis and pushes the new patient into that frame. Hannah starts with the broader evidence and asks which facts do not fit. By the review, Manon has a tidy story; Hannah has a slower but safer question for the attending.
examples.whatToDo: Manon follows the vivid match until it crowds the record. Hannah checks the match against evidence-based medicine and flags the missing facts.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast shows why status is not enough. Two trained readers can diverge when one lets a familiar case lead and the other checks the pattern.

examples.title: A Handrail Sentence
examples.scenario: Ryan's repeat-test order sat in the system, so the Toronto internal medicine talk began after morning rounds in the hospital corridor. He was annoyed that Donald Redelmeier's medical decision-making question had reached his diagnosis. The mentor kept her voice low near the elevators: "A backup for judgment is not an insult to judgment." Ryan heard the reframe and added the missing comparison.
examples.whatToDo: Ryan treats the base-rate check as part of care rather than a challenge to his skill. He adds the comparison before the case becomes settled.
examples.whyItMatters: The reframe protects pride and patients at the same time. Experts can keep their judgment and still build a routine that catches predictable error.

examples.title: The Learner's Confusion
examples.scenario: Sliding the case sheet back across the classroom table, Audrey asks why the decision science workshop keeps mentioning base rates if doctors learn from patients. The instructor writes availability, anchoring, and representativeness on the board. Audrey's confusion becomes the lesson: evidence-based medicine does not erase experience; it checks when one story gets too loud.
examples.whatToDo: Audrey marks the case note with one question: which broader evidence would keep this vivid patient from taking over the diagnosis?
examples.whyItMatters: The learner's mistake is common and useful. Experience matters, but it needs evidence beside it when memory makes one case feel larger than it is.

examples.title: After the New Yorker Link
examples.scenario: The agenda changed after the New Yorker links filled the reading group thread. Earlier, the group treated Cass Sunstein and Richard Thaler as clever commentators on Kahneman and Tversky. Later, with one variable changed, Edouard asked each reader to bring a behavioral economics rule or form that assumes perfect choosers. The talk moved from admiration to design.
examples.whatToDo: Edouard changes the agenda from summary to inspection. Each reader must name where law, policy, or behavioral economics would build a better choice path.
examples.whyItMatters: The before-and-after shows how an idea spreads for real. It is not viral because people praise it; it travels when institutions use it.

questions.prompt: In a hospital orientation, Wallace hears, "Doctors already train for hard cases, so decision research adds little." What does this response miss?
choices: It misses that Redelmeier brought decision research into medicine because diagnosis and triage still require judgment under uncertainty.
It misses that Redelmeier made medicine useful mainly as a memorable example for psychology students.
It misses that Redelmeier showed clinical training should be replaced by outside review in uncertain cases.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 supports the first choice: Redelmeier carried decision research into medicine because clinical work includes uncertain judgment. The other choices turn the medical case into decoration or replacement.

questions.prompt: A resident sees a patient who resembles last week's dramatic case and keeps the first triage label despite mixed evidence. Which bias pattern fits?
choices: The patient resembles a named example, so the judgment deserves more confidence.
A vivid prior case and an early label are dominating attention through availability and anchoring.
The resident is using a clear personal story, so base rates are no longer needed.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 names availability, anchoring, and representativeness in medical judgment. The near misses mistake vividness or naming for proof when both still need source support.

questions.prompt: During a law seminar, Manon says, "Sunstein and Thaler are mostly part of the biography after the main research is done." How should that line be read?
choices: It is right because their role is background color around the friendship.
It is right because behavioral economics belongs outside the decision lesson.
It is wrong because they show the research becoming a base for policy, law, and regulation.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 ties Sunstein and Thaler to policy design and regulation. They are not decorative biography; they show the work moving into institutional thought.

questions.prompt: A medical journal club and a policy group both recognize their own errors in the research. Which reason best explains the spread?
choices: It supplied a rare case that mattered only in the profession where it first appeared.
It explained errors among experts, not only mistakes by untrained subjects.
It turned every profession into a copy of the original psychology experiment.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 says the spread came from explaining expert errors. That makes the mechanism portable without making every field the same as the original setting.

questions.prompt: Hannah says a bias check is just a summary, not a real practice, while reviewing a patient-safety form. Which answer follows from the source fact?
choices: It is just a summary because the final claim does not name a condition that can be tested.
It is just a summary because public errors matter less than private expert confidence.
It is a practice because high-stakes fields need routines when patients, clients, markets, and citizens bear the cost.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 gives the causal hinge: routines matter because other people bear the consequences. The wrong choices erase the concrete condition that makes the claim testable.

questions.prompt: A writer wants to swap Redelmeier's medical scene for any story about a confident expert. What is lost?
choices: The swap is fine because any expert anecdote teaches the same decision lesson.
The verified setting of internal medicine, Toronto, and medical decision-making is what gives the example its force.
The swap is stronger because the mechanism matters less than having a memorable expert.
questions.explanation: Fact 6 says the Redelmeier case is not interchangeable. The hard specifics tie the lesson to clinical harm, not to a generic expert story.

questions.prompt: A policy team reads Kahneman and Tversky, then looks for where a public form assumes perfect choice. Why does this fit the Sunstein and Thaler example?
choices: It adds a distinct route from lab finding to institutional design through behavioral economics.
It repeats the medical case with new wording because one strong example is enough.
It treats policy as biography because decision science stays inside the friendship story.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 supports the policy route: a lab finding becomes institutional design when it predicts public errors. The other choices collapse the second case into repetition or background.

questions.prompt: A clinic moves from one Redelmeier teaching case to evidence-based medicine as a wider practice. What does that move add?
choices: It broadens the idea from one physician to an institution that checks professional judgment against evidence.
It proves broad claims need no concrete institution once the expert is respected.
It shows professional status removes the cognitive weaknesses found in lab subjects.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 says evidence-based medicine broadens the concept and shows professional status does not remove vulnerability. The distractors make the broad claim less verifiable or too flattering.

questions.prompt: A senior regulator says, "Every expert should be second-guessed from outside before acting." What is the stronger reading?
choices: The better reading is that outside second-guessing should replace expert judgment whenever the stakes are high.
The better reading is that a simple anti-expert slogan is safer than a narrow practice.
The better reading is that experts need tools that catch predictable errors before first impressions harden.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 preserves the boundary. The lesson does not reject expertise; it asks experts to use tools before an early impression turns rigid.

reviewCards.front: What does it mean for decision research to leave psychology?
reviewCards.back: It means the ideas start guiding medicine, law, policy, and public design. The errors are no longer only lab findings; they shape real choices made by experts under uncertainty.

reviewCards.front: How can a vivid prior case distort a medical decision?
reviewCards.back: Availability makes the prior case come to mind fast. Anchoring lets the early label pull later evidence toward it. The doctor may see the familiar story before seeing the patient clearly.

reviewCards.front: Why do Sunstein and Thaler matter to the spread of the ideas?
reviewCards.back: They show a second path for the work. A finding about judgment can become institutional design when forms, rules, and defaults are built around predictable public errors.

reviewCards.front: What hard edge keeps the lesson from becoming anti-expert?
reviewCards.back: The lesson is not to distrust all expert judgment. The lesson is to add tools that catch predictable errors before expertise locks onto a first impression.

reviewCards.front: Recall prediction discipline (Ch 7): name one concrete moment here where it actually bites.
reviewCards.back: It bites when a doctor must shrink confidence in a vivid diagnosis back toward evidence and base rates. The patient's chart needs more than the story that feels most like last week.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice catching the first story before it becomes the only story. Write a one-line backup note that names the early label, vivid case, or familiar pattern pulling your judgment. Then ask what evidence would still matter if that first story were wrong.

ifThenPlans.context: When a case feels familiar fast
ifThenPlans.plan: If today's case reminds you of a vivid recent case, then write the similarity and one missing difference before you act.

ifThenPlans.context: When someone else bears the cost
ifThenPlans.plan: If your call affects a patient, client, market, or citizen, then add one check that would catch a first-impression error.

ifThenPlans.context: When a check feels like an insult
ifThenPlans.plan: If a bias check feels like an attack on your skill, then write the line, "This protects the judgment, not my pride."

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before one important decision in the next 24 hours, write one line: "The label, case, or pattern pulling me is ___." Then look for one fact it hides.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For seven days, keep a daily judgment-backup log with three columns: first story, check used, and what changed. Review the column that repeats most.

memorableLines.text: A vivid case can crowd out the quiet base rate.
Expertise needs backup when the first story feels too easy.
